newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungarian farmers renew blockade before govt talks.
newsitem.headline: Hungarian farmers renew blockade before govt talks.

text.p: Hungary's government faced new roadblocks on Wednesday as protesting farmers looked beyond tax complaints to demand an overhaul of the country's battered agriculture sector.
"The government just won't listen to reason," Huba Kozma, head of farmers' association MAGOSZ, told Reuters. "They will only bow to pressure".

A series of roadblocks were thrown up last week in central Hungary by an ad-hoc group of farmers from Kiskoros to protest against increased taxes. The farmers have since formed their own organisation, MTESZ.
Their leader, Gyula Kosa, claims to represent the interests of millions of Hungarians who work the land, but there are about a dozen such organisations, often with conflicting goals.
Last Tuesday, the government accepted most changes the Kiskoros protesters asked for. But the protesters now seem to want more out of Wednesday's new round of talks with government officials.
However, Kosa refused to outline what demands he would deliver to Prime Minister Gyula Horn, Finance Minister Peter Medgyessy and Agriculture Minister Frigyes Nagy.
"It would be premature to disclose our position ahead of the talks," he said.
The protest is due to start at 0800 GMT, and is scheduled to last until the group comes to an agreement with the government, or, in case of failure, until the end of next week.

The MAGOSZ protest is scheduled to start on March 10 and is designed to give weight to a 12-point list of demands, including a government guarantee of an eight to 10 percent profit margin on farming, protective import duties and the suspension of this year's new tax regulations.
Agriculture Minister Nagy is expected to deliver the draft of a comprehensive medium-term agricultural programme on Thursday, which the government says would deal with most farmers' demands.
Both MAGOSZ and MTESZ said however that they were not even shown the draft.
"I have no idea what it will contain," Kosa said.
Before coming to power in 1994, Hungary's Socialist Party promised to streamline the country's agriculture sector, but they have yet to make significant headway.

Since the collapse of communism, food consumption, livestock and agricultural productivity have been in steady decline. Nagy, the fifth person to hold the agriculture portfolio in six years, concedes these flaws.
"Agriculture is in crisis, but not in an impossible situation," he said last month.

Nagy and Hungary's government face a difficult balancing act as they try to keep a tight rein on costs in the run-up to eventual European Union membership, while at the same time avoiding upsetting farmers ahead of a 1998 general election.
The task is further complicated by the farmers' reluctance to provide even the most basic information about their incomes, their crops or the size of their holdings.
Prime Minister Gyula Horn said on Tuesday that only 13,000 of Hungary's 1.5 million farmers submitted an income tax return in 1995.
